data.title: Starlink AI Acquisition in Deal to Take Spider Digital Technology Public
data.description:
By Stephen Nakrosis

Blank-check company Starlink AI Acquisition said it entered an agreement to take Spider Digital Technology, an operator of a cryptocurrency mining pool, public.

The deal assigns Spider Digital a valuation of $250 million for purposes of determining the merger consideration, the companies said.

Spider Digital has headquarters in Singapore, and is a technology company dedicated to blockchain research and ecosystem development, it said. The company has concentrated on cryptocurrency mining pool operations and operates its own proprietary mining pool system and maintains independent block generation capabilities, it added.

The deal is subject to approval from shareholders, New York Stock Exchange listing approval and other closing conditions.

Write to Stephen Nakrosis at stephen.nakrosis@wsj.com

data.title: Can Shopping Ever Be Fun Again? At Trunk Shows, the Answer Is Yes — WSJ
data.description:
By Chantal Fernandez | Photography by Amy Lombard for WSJ

On a recent Friday morning at a barn in Bedford, N.Y., I was on my hands and knees with two dozen other women as our fitness instructor, Carolynn Scull, reminded us we had more than endorphins to look forward to after 45 minutes of pulsing our limbs in the air.

"Guys, c'mon, you have champagne and beautiful, beautiful coats waiting for you!" said Scull, whose popular Pilates-inspired classes usually cost $55 a pop. That day, she was leading a complimentary workout at the Bedford Post Inn as a warm-up to a "shopping experience" — otherwise known as a trunk show — co-hosted by Max Mara, the Italian label known for camel-wool coats that can cost upward of $3,000.

After the class, I walked with sweaty would-be shoppers into a room with more than a dozen racks displaying capes, coats, jackets and knit dresses. A calligrapher was there to personalize free gifts with purchases, while two baristas manned an espresso bar set up for the occasion. Upstairs, Pilar DeMann, a makeup artist, was offering free eyebrow shaping services.

"I could walk into 10 stores and not buy anything," said Kerri Fitzpatrick, a 38-year-old shopper from Rye Brook, N.Y, after handing over her credit card to be swiped for a $1,860 furry black cape. "But when I'm at an event like this, I just feel like it's special."

Everything but the trunk

Decades ago, trunk shows involved designers like Bill Blass and Oscar de la Renta bringing actual trunks filled with embroidered gowns and luncheon-ready skirt suits to department stores and boutiques in major cities, where customers could place advance orders for the next season's clothes.

Now, as many department stores struggle to keep locations open, and as suburbs have grown wealthier, trunk shows are popping up in new places and taking new forms. No longer just events where designers use trunks full of samples to sell preorders, many combine the instant gratification of off-the-rack shopping with exclusive locations — private homes, hotels, yachts — and free perks.

The trunk shows at Laura Vinroot Poole's independent boutique Capitol, which has locations in Los Angeles and Charlotte, N.C., often feature live entertainment: Invited guests who shop can also watch Poole interview designers for her podcast. "They can come, have a juice or a tea, learn something, and then be more connected to a designer," she said.

Appearances by designers or brand insiders are still largely a component of modern trunk shows. Rubbing elbows with shoppers at the Bedford Post Inn were Max Mara USA's chief executive, Riccardo Broggi, and his wife.

The label hired City Country Beach, an agency that organizes private luxury experiences, to curate the guest list and set the program. "It's not just a bunch of racks and clothing," Jaimee Marano Lunderborg, City Country Beach co-founder, said of their events, which the agency doesn't call trunk shows.

Marano Lunderborg and Lizzi Bickford Meadow started the business in 2019 to advise brands on how to reach elite shoppers, especially those who had moved outside major cities. City Country Beach has since worked with labels including TWP, Balmain and Bulgari on events in places like Grosse Pointe, Mich. and Nantucket, Mass.

The agency now organizes about 50 events a year, according to its co-founders. Each relies on at least one well-connected local host, who invites their friends and family and is typically rewarded with a shopping credit.

Less scrolling, more shopping

Jennifer Galante Han, a digital strategy consultant, used the trunk-show model for La Volta, the consignment and vintage business she started earlier this year. At one of her first trunk shows, held in the private lounge of an upscale building in Manhattan's Tribeca neighborhood, Galante Han sold five-figures worth of luxury handbags and designer clothing in two hours, she said.

Her events have not had perks as lavish as others. But they have tapped into the social aspect of trunk shows, which has made them more compelling at a time when the internet has disrupted how we browse and socialize.

"Women want to shop together," Galante Han said, recalling the days when she would walk around malls with her friends growing up. Now, she added, "you're scrolling at midnight on your phone, and you're texting people, 'What do you think of this?' "

Zoe Gauntlett, whose business, Untold Luxury Group, uses trunk shows and personal shoppers to connect luxury brands with customers, said that group shopping can often inspire impulse buying.

For smaller or emerging labels, trunk shows are also opportunities to be discovered. Gauntlett specifically looks for brands that shoppers "wouldn't be able to walk into a department store and ordinarily see."

Independent designer Amir Taghi has had a front-row seat to the trunk-show revival. He started hosting them when he introduced his line of colorful, feminine womenswear in 2018. "It was kind of archaic," he said. "Now, all the brands are doing it, no matter what level they are."

Taghi generates most of his revenue through trunk shows: this year, sales at his events have totaled more than $1.5 million. On a busy month, he holds up to eight in six cities, attending most himself. His upscale clothes, priced between $800 and $3,600, are more popular in places like San Antonio and Aspen, Colo., than in New York.

Like others, Taghi typically taps local hosts for his trunk shows and thanks them with shopping credits. "There are some women, no matter how wealthy they are, that want a discount."

data.title: Fitch Cuts France's Outlook to Negative on Weaker Growth, Widening Deficit — Update
data.description:
By Stephen Nakrosis

Fitch Ratings lowered its outlook on France's credit rating to negative from stable, as the country faces economic and social pressure over its debt and growing borrowing costs.

Fitch said the negative outlook reflects a deterioration since its August review, and cited weaker growth, higher borrowing costs and a wider deficit. These factors are worsening debt dynamics from an already weak starting point, Fitch added.

Yields on France's government bonds have also risen since the last review, Fitch said. The agency said it now forecasts interest payments will increase to 3.3% of GDP in 2028 from 2.5% of GDP in 2025. Fitch also sees France's deficit at 5.5% of GDP in 2027, which it said reflects a weaker growth assessment and the risk of concessions during the budget process.

The next scheduled review date for France's rating hasn't yet been set, Fitch said, but added it expects to review the rating by end-February 2027 at the latest.

France's public debt is closing on 120% of its GDP, and the nation's economy shrank in the third quarter. The government is expecting the deficit to hit 5.4% of GDP this year.

In recent weeks, hundreds of thousands of people have taken to the streets of Paris and other French cities, with some protesters resorting to vandalism and violence.

Right-wing presidential candidate Marine Le Pen has recently cast herself as a unifying figure, and far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon has vowed to cancel hundreds of billions of euros in French national debt, The Wall Street Journal reported.

Last week, Moody's Ratings kept its Aa3 credit rating on France unchanged, citing the country's diversified economy and strong public institutions. However, Moody's retained its negative outlook on the country as France continues to face political instability and protests.

Moody's retains a higher rating than peers Fitch and S&P Global Ratings. S&P had lowered France's rating to A+ in October of last year.

Fitch affirmed the country's A+ rating, which it said is supported by a large, wealthy and diversified economy, strong institutions, euro area membership and a resilient banking sector.

data.title: Exxon plans to spend $10B on refining business to boost margins, CEO says
data.description:
ExxonMobil plans to spend more than $100B through 2030 to boost global energy supplies, including ~10% focused on its refining business, particularly at its existing facilities, including the Baton Rouge, Louisiana, and Beaumont, Texas, refineries, to improve production yields and raise refined product margins, CEO Darren Woods said Friday.

The CEO said Exxon has been investing "selectively" in its large refineries that have portfolios of high-value production like lubricants, chemicals, and petroleum products, the CEO said in the company's earnings conference call.

"We will continue to look for ways that we can leverage existing facilities to continue to make products that have high margins, high value in the short term," Woods said, adding that investing in existing refineries allows the company to increase production capacity at roughly half the cost compared with building a brand-new facility.

Exxon expects its investments across its U.S. refineries will raise distillate production by another 100K bbl/day, the CEO said on the call, without providing a specific time period.

"Diesel is the key crunch point here because it is so critical to economic growth and [has] very inelastic demand," Woods said during an appearance on CNBC. "The demand for diesel remains high despite the capacity."

Woods said the company has achieved record levels of utilization for its refineries, and the yield of diesel across its global refining footprint is at record levels.

"It's all been a function of trying to drive more product into the marketplace to meet that demand and to drive costs down," the CEO told CNBC.

Exxon shares closed up 2.1% on Friday, scoring an all-time intraday high of $188.50, after reporting $15.4B in Q3 profit, more than double its earnings a year earlier, with its refining business earning a record $9.05B, nearly 5x higher than a year ago.

data.title: Big Homes, Big Loans — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Beckie Strum

America's wealthy house hunters are brushing off higher mortgage rates. In fact, demand for multimillion-dollar loans is booming. Originations over $5 million spiked more than 50% last year compared with 2024, according to Home Mortgage Disclosure Act data provided by the Mortgage Bankers Association.

The trend has persisted, say private bankers, who have seen elevated demand for multimillion-dollar loans since last year. The spike in so-called superjumbo loans defies the narrative that the ultrarich just pay cash. "It's a little bit unexpected," said Jon Kessler, head of Credit & Cash Management Solutions at PNC Private Bank. "We had a view that maybe this activity would fall off a little bit due to the rising rate environment, but it has been fairly consistent and fairly strong."

A booming stock market explains some of the trend. The S&P 500 index is up 12% this year; investors figure that's a much better return than tying up cash in a mansion.

The big loan spike mirrors big-ticket home sales last year: $5 million-plus transactions increased 8%, per Realtor.com. (News Corp, which owns Barron's, operates Realtor.com via its Move unit.) Wealthy house hunters are benefiting from a softening market, while average buyers get "crushed" by mortgage rates, said Joel Berner, a senior economist at Realtor.com. The crush should continue along with the superjumbos.

Write to Beckie Strum at beckie.strum@dowjones.com

Last Week

Scary AI

Markets were gripped with fear about the AI trade after Alphabet stock notched its worst day ever. Scarier still were stumbles from Intel and Amazon.com — not to mention Nvidia's spy scandal. (See below.) The small-cap Russell 2000 may be looking good right now. Maybe...

From Beijing, With Love

One of the more bizarre stories of the week: The New York Times, followed by others, reported that a Singapore data-center exec may be a Beijing asset. And that she "had developed a close relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang." The kicker: President Donald Trump was briefed a while ago, but didn't act on it. Nvidia responded to the Times, in part: "Meetings with customers are a part of a CEO's job."

No-Layoff Layoffs

Microsoft plans to offer buyouts to 60,000 employees. (Gotta pay for Mr. AI.) It wouldn't call the get-out-of Redmond packages "layoffs." But if they don't reach a big enough number, you won't need AI to figure out what happens next.

Lawyer Up

Reports have been flying that Trump government officials and businesses are, in anticipation of the Democrats winning control of Congress, reaching out to consultants and law firms for help. They fear retribution. (Hmm, why?) But as the Journal pointed out, some companies are preparing for a possible handover the old-fashioned way: sending cash to Democrat political committees.

Next Week

Monday 11/2

Apple, Palantir Technologies, and Vertex Pharmaceuticals release earnings on Monday, followed by Advanced Micro Devices, Amgen, Booking Holdings, and Pfizer on Tuesday. CVS Health, McDonald's, Qualcomm, and Uber Technologies report their results on Wednesday, while Airbnb and ConocoPhillips do?the same on Thursday.

The Institute for Supply Management releases its Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index for October. Consensus estimate is for a 54.7 reading, slightly higher than in September.

Tuesday 11/3

American voters head to the polls for the midterm elections, with congressional power at stake. Republicans currently hold a slim majority in the House of Representatives and Senate. Polling suggests that Democrats are a sizable favorite to retake control of the House, while the Senate is closer to a coin flip.

Friday 11/6

The Bureau of Labor Statistics releases the jobs report for October. Economists forecast a 62,000 increase in nonfarm payrolls, after a 29,000 gain in September. The unemployment rate is expected to remain unchanged at 4.2%.

The Numbers

$40 T

Anthropic's view of its market, as suggested in its IPO filing; it's the same size as the national debt.

$0

AI's financial payoff so far to corporate America beyond tech firms, per economist Torsten Sløk.

$31.6 B

Decline in Alphabet co-founder Larry Page's net worth, 11%, as a result of the firm's stock tumble on Oct. 29.

13.9 M

Homes that older households may sell in the next 10 years, 34% above the past decade's pace for seniors' sales.

Write to editors@barrons.com
